analytic.title: Genetic evidence confirms presence of Andean bears in Argentina

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The Andean bear (Tremarctos ornatus) is found throughout the Andes Mountains from Venezuela to Bolivia. However, little is known about its distribution and range in southern areas, including Argentina. Our objective was to develop a genetic marker to identify this species by analysis of non-invasive samples (i.e., hair or feces). We designed a primer pair to amplify a 115-base-pair fragment within cytochrome b of mitochondrial DNA. We successfully amplified the expected fragment in samples from Argentina (collected during 2 periods [1993 and between 2006 and 2008]) having sequences highly similar to Andean bear reference sequences in GenBank; and we identified 2 haplotypes in samples from northwest Argentina. We confirmed the presence of Andean bears in Argentina, which extends the known southern distributional limit about 150 km. Further studies employing our approach will allow for a comprehensive assessment of the potential distribution and southernmost range of this species.

The Andean bear (Tremarctos ornatus) is the only extant species within subfamily Tremarctinae. It has been categorized as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List, and is threatened with extinction because of decreasing population numbers (Goldstein et al. 2008). This bear is endemic to the tropical Andes and is adapted to most biomes present in this subregion (Cavelier et al. 2011). It inhabits areas of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia (Yerena and Torres 1994, Peyton et al. 1998, Yerena 1998, Figueroa and Stucchi 2009), but the extent of its southern range is controversial (Garcı ´a-Rangel 2012). The lack of conclusive data on its southern range makes it difficult to develop realistic and accurate management plans for the species' conservation, or to monitor changes in populations or their distribution (Goldstein et al. 2006). The long-debated presence of this species in northwestern Argentina provides a good example of how lack of conclusive data compromises our understanding of its distribution and range (Garcı ´a-Rangel 2012).

Residents of Bolivia near the Argentina border have reported seeing Andean bear, which has led to several studies suggesting that its presence in northern Argentina is likely (Mares et al. 1989, Ojeda and Mares 1989, Dı ´az et al. 2000). For example, Brown and Rumiz (1989) found signs of Andean bear activities close to Baritu ´National Park (Argentina). More recently, Del Moral and Bracho (2009) and Del Moral and Lameda Camacaro (2011) provided similar indirect evidence of presence of the species in Argentina, including descriptions of tracks, food remains, and scat. These records, however, were not definitive, suggesting need for additional supportive data. Rumiz et al. (2012) further suggested that the evidence for the Andean bear's presence in Argentina is inconclusive. These authors reviewed diverse publications with data from .800 survey sites in the same region, which used camera traps to monitor species including felids, primates, and tapir, as well as species richness. The extensive surveying done in these studies, however, did not show evidence of Andean bear presence (Rumiz et al. 2012). These authors suggested use of non-invasive DNA analysis to confirm species presence in surveyed areas. Non-invasive genetic sampling (i.e., hair and feces samples) can provide conclusive evidence on species presence and may provide important information for conservation of rare and elusive species (Beja-Pereira et al. 2009).

DNA retrieved from non-invasive samples is often altered and degraded in a way similar to ancient DNA, making its analysis more complex than with DNA from tissue samples (Page `s et al. 2009). These samples, however, contain both nuclear and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), the latter of which is present at a higher copy number per cell (Waits and Paetkau 2005). Consequently, success rates in detecting sequences in mtDNA are greater than in studies analyzing nuclear sequences. In addition, analysis using non-invasive sampling methods has been refined for analysis of short mtDNA fragments (200 base-pairs [bp] or shorter), further improving success (Teletchea et al. 2008). The cytochrome b gene in the mitochondrial genome is a useful marker for vertebrate species identification, particularly in degraded samples (Teletchea et al. 2008, Chaves et al. 2012). Conserved sequences are found in regions of mtDNA, allowing for amplification of short fragments using universal vertebrate primers. There are also regions with interspecies sequence diversity, but with little or no intraspecific variation such as that in cytochrome b. Furthermore, cytochrome b sequences are readily available in GenBank for comparison and taxonomic identification of DNA samples (Wayne et al. 1997, Farrell et al. 2000, Irwin 2002, Janec ˇka et al. 2008, Teletchea et al. 2008, Chaves et al. 2012, Rodgers and Janec ˇka 2013).

We developed a cytochrome b-based assay to determine the taxonomic identity of environmental DNA present in feces and hair thought to be of the Andean bear. Our goal was to determine whether the Andean bear was present in northwestern Argentina. 2011) are represented as stars. div.head: Study area
div.p: We conducted the study in the Yungas Forest ecosystem (Cabrera and Willink 1980), which is part of the tropical Andes ecoregion. We selected areas by taking into account their protection status, reported sightings of Andean bears by local people, and evidence of bear activities from previous reports. The areas were within the Yungas Biosphere Reserve (13,287 km 2 ; Fig. 1). One sampling area was in the Santa Maria mountains (23u209-23u219S, 64u419-64u439W), a 126km 2 area at 700-1,000-m elevation; and the second area sampled was Ramada Barrosa (23u459-23u479S, 65u079-65u109W), a 50-km 2 area at 900-1,910-m elevation. Annual rainfall ranges from 1,000 to 1,800 mm, with 95% occurring in summer (Bianchi and Yan ˜ez 1992).

div.head: Methods
div.p: We collected feces and hair samples during 2 periods using different sampling methods and storage conditions. In 1993, 3 samples (2 fecal and 1 hair sample) were collected by Dr. A. Canedi. These samples were stored in the Estacio ´n de Fauna Silvestre Martı ´n Vucetich collection at Universidad Nacional de Jujuy (A. Canedi, Estacio ´n de Fauna Silvestre, Universidad Nacional de Jujuy, personal communication). Remaining samples were collected by our team between 2006 and 2008 using systematic surveys of the Yungas Biosphere Reserve, an area of approximately 180 km 2 . We surveyed about 100 km with transects of 5-20 km. We searched for bear scat and hair on foot or by horseback, and occasionally used tracking dogs. We established transects along mountain peaks, because Andean bear activity trails are commonly found in these areas elsewhere in its range (Figueroa andStucchi 2009, Castellanos 2011). We collected samples that appeared to be Andean bear feces or hair (Fig. 2) and stored them in 15-mL or 50-mL tubes containing 10-g or 20-g silica gel beads, respectively (Nsubuga et al. 2004). Nine of the samples collected were selected for analysis based on collection date, sample quantity, and avoiding samples that appeared degraded.

We developed a method for Andean bear species identification using DNA isolated from non-invasive samples. We designed polymerase chain reaction (PCR) primers to specifically amplify cytochrome b sequences in T. ornatus mtDNA using sequence data from GenBank (Zhang and Ryder 1993, Talbot and Shields 1996, Yu et al. 2007, Krause et al. 2008, Benson et al. 2010). We designed a primer pair using Primer3Plus (Untergasser et al. 2007) to amplify a fragment within the cytochrome b gene (TOCYTB FW 59-GACCTCC-CAACACCATCAAA-39 and TOCYTB RV 59-CTC-GACAGATATGGGCGACT-39). The predicted amplicon size was 155 bp, and because primers span 40 bp, informative sequences are the central 115 bp.

We isolated DNA from fecal (20-30 mg) and hair (7-30 hair follicles) samples using the DNeasy Tissue Extraction Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) or ZR Soil Microbe DNA MicroPrep TM (Zymo Research, Orange, California, USA) following manufacturer's instructions. We conducted PCRs in 20 mL with 1x Immomix PCR Buffer (Bioline Reagents, London, England, United Kingdom), 0.5 pM of each primer, and 80-100 ng DNA extract. We used thermal cycling with an initial denaturation at 95uC for 10 minutes, followed by 40 cycles of 30 seconds at 95uC, 1 minute at 56uC and 1 minute at 72uC, and a final extension for 15 minutes at 72uC. We conducted 2 replicates for each PCR, and all experiments included negative controls.

We compared sequences with those in GenBank using BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) search algorithm (Altschul et al. 1990). Sequences having .80% similarity with our cytochrome b sequences were aligned and compared using Clustal W in Mega 5.10 (Tamura et al. 2011); alignments for all haplotypes were unambiguous. We performed phylogenetic reconstruction using maximum likelihood in MEGA 5.10 (Tamura et al. 2011). For the maximum-likelihood tree, we conducted bootstrap analysis with 10,000 replicates as a measure of support for the clades obtained. We treated gaps as missing data using the method of complete deletion. We used a maximum-likelihood search level of 1, the Nearest-Neighbor Interchange on random trees as the tree search method, and the automatic initial tree with very strong branch swap filter (Tamura et al. 2011). We developed the tree using a condensed tree with a topology cut-off value for consensus equal to 50%.

div.head: Results
div.p: Six (2 fecal and 4 hair samples) of 9 samples analyzed were successfully amplified (Table 1). The sampling sites were about 150 km south of the reported range for the species (Goldstein et al. 2008; Fig. 1). Two haplotypes for Andean bear cytochrome b sequences were identified (Table 1). Five samples (ANI30-3, ANI31-3, ANI32, FM1, FM3) had 100% identity with T. ornatus sequences haplotype 1 (H1; Zhang and Ryder 1993, Yu et al. 2007, Krause et al. 2008) by BLAST analysis. Sample FM 7 from Salta represented a new haplotype (H2) assigned to T. ornatus with 96% similarity corresponding to 4 unique changes, all transitions (Appendix 1). The occurrence of this haplotype was confirmed with 2 replicates in different PCR assays. Highest sequence similarity in non-Ursidae mammalian species in fragments amplified were those of white-lipped peccary (Tayassu pecari), with 88% Andean bear sequence identity. Phylogenetic analysis showed that haplotypes obtained from Jujuy and Salta's samples constitute a clade with other Ursidae species, and the node had strong bootstrap support (85%; Fig. 3).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Whereas previous reports described Andean bear sign and reports from local people (which are subject to misidentification), our results provide compelling scientific documentation that Andean bears occur in Argentina and .150 km further south than previously thought. The small cytochrome b fragment (115 bp) we described was suitable for identification of Andean bears, even in samples containing degraded DNA. Though the phylogenetic analysis highlights the identity of the Andean bear cytochrome b sequence, the tree obtained does not necessarily reflect the evolutionary relationship of species analyzed (Pamilo and Nei 1988). Phylogeographic analysis of the Andean bear using mtDNA markers could provide useful information on the extent of genetic diversity in its geographic distribution (DeYoung and Honeycutt 2005). Such information could be used to help establish appropriate conservation units and better understand genetic relationships between Argentinean and Bolivian populations. Unfortunately, information on the origin from the wild of the 5 reference sequences from GenBank included in our phylogenetic analysis was not reported (Zhang and Ryder 1993, Talbot and Shields 1996, Yu et al. 2007, Krause et al. 2008).

Mitochondrial DNA is inherited by maternal lineage, and thus the probability of distinguishing individuals with this marker is very low, such that estimating number of animals sampled using mtDNA yields conservative estimates (DeYoung and Honeycutt 2005). Analysis of our 6 samples suggests the presence of 2-4 bears. The 2 samples from the southernmost site were collected 15 years apart; therefore, they likely represent at most 2 bears. Among the 4 samples from the northern sites, 2 haplotypes were identified, representing .2 individuals.

A more accurate measure or estimate of individual numbers in Argentinean samples can be obtained using microsatellite markers (Selkoe and Toonen 2006, Da Fontoura-Rodrigues et al. 2008, Viteri and Waits 2009, Sharma et al. 2013). A number of population genetics studies that have included estimates of T. ornatus population size have been reported. These studies made use of microsatellite loci originally cloned from domestic dogs (Canis lupus familiaris), brown bears (Ursus arctos), and black bears (U. americanus; Ruiz-Garcia 2003, Ruiz-Garcia et al. 2005, Viteri andWaits 2009). Developing the use of these markers for extending our study will depend on bear non-invasive samples and their amplification success.

The Andean bear moves along an altitudinal gradient that includes several different habitat types, following seasonal patterns of food resources (Peyton 1980, Suarez 1988, Cuesta et al. 2003, Paisley and Garshelis 2006, Goldstein et al. 2008). Several anthropogenic activities that have modified the landscape also modify effective habitat availability for the bear as well as its dispersal behavior (Garcı ´a-Rangel 2012). The regions of Santa Cruz, Chuquisaca, and parts of Tarija in Bolivia and northern Argentina have undergone drastic changes in land use, including significant loss of forest (Killeen et al. 2007, Clark et al. 2012). Habitat loss or food availability could involve changes in geographic distribution of the Andean bear and may explain its presence in Argentina. Therefore, the presence of bears in northern Argentina would not necessarily be due to population expansion. Consequently, it will be important to conduct an intensive sampling effort in potential distribution areas already identified in the Bolivian Yungas and Chaco Serrano forest (Velez-Liendo et al. 2013) and also include potential distribution areas in the same ecoregion system in Argentina.

Our study provides further insights involving noninvasive sample collection and molecular tools to detect and study Andean bears (see Garshelis 2006, McKelvey et al. 2006). We used a short fragment within the mtDNA cytochrome b gene to confirm the occurrence of Andean bear in a debated area of its geographic range in northwest Argentina (Brown and Rumiz 1989, Mares et al. 1989, Ojeda and Mares 1989, Dı ´az et al. 2000, Del Moral and Bracho 2009, Jayat et al. 2009, Del Moral and Lameda Camacaro 2011, Rumiz et al. 2012). We recommend collection of additional samples to better determine the presence and distribution of Andean bears in Argentina. Meanwhile, the occurrence of this flagship species in Argentina's Yungas ecoregion underlies the need to develop and implement conservation policies to preserve the biodiversity of this region.
